analysis.one_liner: Keeps home care aides exempt from minimum wage and overtime pay rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 17 Republican cosponsors, was referred to the Senate labor committee in June 2012 and died there without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Companionship Exemption Protection Act would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to preserve the long-standing exemption that lets employers of home care and companionship workers — including staffing agencies, not just families — pay those workers no overtime and, in some cases, less than minimum wage. It would lock detailed definitions of "companionship services" and "third-party employment" into the statute, so agency-employed home care aides remain exempt, and it would strip the Labor Secretary's authority to define the exemption by regulation — directly countering the Obama-era Labor Department rulemaking that sought to extend minimum wage and overtime protections to home care workers. The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Home care agencies, staffing companies, and other third-party employers would gain, because the bill preserves their ability to pay home care aides without overtime and, in some cases, below minimum wage — and it would do so in statute, removing the Labor Secretary's power to change the rules by regulation. Some families paying for in-home care would benefit from continued lower labor costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Home care agencies and staffing companies

how_it_helps.text: It would write the minimum wage and overtime exemption for companionship services into the Fair Labor Standards Act itself and strike the part of current law that leaves the definition up to the Secretary of Labor, blocking the Department of Labor's then-pending rule to extend protections to home care workers.

It defines companionship services broadly to include non-medical in-home care and related household work — meal preparation, laundry, bathing, assistance with incontinence, medication reminders — and explicitly covers workers employed by an agency rather than by the family, keeping those aides exempt from wage and hour rules.
By excluding only care performed by trained medical personnel such as nurses, it would keep the exemption for the bulk of the home care workforce employed through third-party agencies.

analysis.who_pays: Home care aides — mostly low-wage women, many employed by agencies — would bear the cost, remaining ineligible for overtime pay and, in some cases, minimum wage. Turnover and burnout in this workforce also affect the quality and continuity of care that elderly and disabled people receive.

drawbacks.text: Preserving the exemption means home care aides — who assist with bathing, incontinence, meal preparation, and medication reminders, and who are often employed by agencies rather than families — could continue to work long hours with no overtime pay, and in some cases below minimum wage.

Supporters' best argument is that minimum wage and overtime rules for in-home care could raise the cost of care for families and reduce flexible, live-in, or irregular arrangements that some elderly and disabled people and their families prefer.

The exemption has existed since 1938 and preserving it through statute, rather than leaving definitions to the Labor Secretary, would make it much harder for any future administration to extend basic wage protections to home care workers by regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's strongest argument is that extending overtime rules to third-party home care could raise costs for agencies and families and complicate flexible scheduling in a field built on irregular hours. But the cost of preserving the exemption falls on a workforce that is overwhelmingly low-paid, and an exemption that lets third-party employers avoid both minimum wage and overtime is hard to defend on its own terms. Weighing the two, the bill would have traded continued underpayment of home care aides for lower care bills — a trade whose cost is borne by the workers themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in June 2012, and the committee never took it up before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Johanns introduced S. 3280 on June 7, 2012, joined by 12 initial Republican cosponsors and 17 total Republican cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on June 7, 2012.
No further action was taken: the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Home care aides came out ahead, because the bill that would have kept them exempt from minimum wage and overtime never advanced; the Labor Department's rule extending those protections ultimately took effect. Agencies that wanted the exemption written into statute lost that opportunity.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Home care aides, not the agencies

for.name: Mike Johanns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 7, 2012 to preserve the companionship services exemption and strip the Labor Secretary's regulatory authority over it.

for.name: 17 of 47 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Alexander, Boozman, Coburn, Corker, Cornyn, Enzi, Isakson, Portman, Rubio, Snowe, Chambliss, and Burr.

against.name: Tom Harkin
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the committee held no hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Department of Labor (Obama administration)
against.what_they_did: Had proposed a rule in late 2011 to extend minimum wage and overtime protections to third-party employed home care workers; the bill was written to override that rulemaking, and the rule ultimately took effect in 2015.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-led committee the bill sat in never acted on it; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill locks in these agencies' ability to pay home care aides without overtime and, in some cases, below minimum wage, keeping their largest cost — labor — artificially low. It would do this by statute, blocking the Labor Department rule that would have extended wage protections to their workers.

Families and wealthier households using nannies, aides, and other domestic help would keep paying without overtime obligations under the preserved exemption. The benefit to them comes at the expense of the workers in their homes.
